record_deal.q: What was the exact moment you decided to walk away from the record deal?
record_deal.a: I decided to turn off my phone, computer and TV for 10 days and then make a decision. I thought about it long and hard and decided not to sign it when I read what it actually would mean for my life. No creative freedom. Not being able to pick my own band members.

record_deal.q: Before the record deal, how did you get into music?
record_deal.a: Queen. Greatest Hits Album. Listened to that a lot. My dad also was a DJ back in the day with vinyls at the parties he would bring his speaker and vinyls. He later sold his vinyls to start his business and provide for our family. I started with a fake guitar and singing. I sang in bands in school, in the church when I was younger, leading worship.

record_deal.q: How did the record deal experience shape your view of the music industry?
record_deal.a: That it was all a business and that it was not a business that was mainly made to make the artists' money but to make the big corporations money.

record_deal.q: Did you ever regret walking away?
record_deal.a: Sure I may have dreamt about what could have been, but I never regretted my actual decision. I was also very young and I don't think I would've been strong enough to face all the temptations that come with a life as a rockstar.

record_deal.q: What's one song you wrote back then that you still think about?
record_deal.a: For my EP I would cover hits from other countries that never went viral in the Netherlands, like Marco Borsato did. We recorded 5 songs like this, one of them was 'Terug Naar Het Begin'.

record_deal.q: What would you say to a 21-year-old offered a record deal?
record_deal.a: You've made the right decision by not signing.

record_deal.q: What did your family and friends say when you walked away?
record_deal.a: My family and friends understood. My band not so much, since we worked together to accomplish this, but they also didn't understand that the record label only wanted me and not them.

dream_or_donate.q: What was the first campaign that made you think it would work?
dream_or_donate.a: There was a girl who needed a wheelchair because she had Fibromyalgia. She raised a few thousand euros in a relatively short amount of time.

dream_or_donate.q: How did you go from musician to building a crowdfunding platform?
dream_or_donate.a: I wrote down a sentence: 'I want to change the world from my living room.' That sentence was 6 months after I decided not to sign the record deal. And 1 year after that we launched Dream or Donate.

dream_or_donate.q: At the peak, what did your daily life look like?
dream_or_donate.a: It wasn't so much about Dream or Donate. It never made me any money. I had many other businesses that were making me money. Crypto, website building businesses, marketing and the main money maker was me being a high-ticket and mindset coach.

dream_or_donate.q: What mistake did you make scaling Dream or Donate?
dream_or_donate.a: I didn't know anything about marketing when I got started. I just thought if I'd build a website people would come, but it needs a lot of marketing.

dream_or_donate.q: How did the media coverage feel?
dream_or_donate.a: The whole country hated me and had an opinion about me. They just believed the media's story. I was 'cancelled' before they started calling it 'cancelling'.

dream_or_donate.q: What did you learn about human generosity?
dream_or_donate.a: That was the whole idea about the crowdfunding platform: giving without expecting anything in return.

the_fall.q: Walk me through the day you found out the platform was hacked.
the_fall.a: The hackers started blackmailing me, because they knew I had a lot of bitcoins so I started giving my bitcoins until I had none left. I was already in a bad situation with wrong people around me, working too hard and my relationship didn't go well.

the_fall.q: What was the worst moment of the cancellation?
the_fall.a: Media was around my house 24/7 with big camera crews and biker gangs wanted to beat me up, because they thought they were entitled to do that.

the_fall.q: How did you decide to sell everything to pay people back?
the_fall.a: Because it was the right thing to do.

the_fall.q: What did you keep after selling everything?
the_fall.a: I tried keeping a wooden gypsy caravan with a tractor. But I eventually had to sell that too.

the_fall.q: Describe a typical day living in the campervan in Tenerife.
the_fall.a: Get up, drink some coffee, go out busking, swim in the ocean, eat some food, do some more busking, maybe organise a party somewhere and sometimes make food on the fire on the beach and then do it all over again.
Not being around my kids or family.

the_fall.q: How did you make money to survive?
the_fall.a: Always music. I also started a spiritual school to help other people get out of depression, called Senang School and had 1200 students within a year. I became a sort of guru, but it felt fake to me at some point so I decided to shut it down and then I started busking.

faith.q: What was the specific moment you found faith?
faith.a: I was in my campervan and I prayed to Jesus on my knees that I wanted to be happy again, like I was as a child, without fame, status, money, drugs or alcohol. That's when everything started changing.

faith.q: How did you quit smoking after 15 years?
faith.a: I asked Jesus to help me.

faith.q: What does 'holy rave' mean to you?
faith.a: It's a place of connection, where people come together and meet each other in the Name of Jesus. To hangout, not to get drunk or high (although you can have a drink), but to meet others and because of the biblically inspired music, you automatically have other conversations and thoughts.

faith.q: Has faith changed how you think about money?
faith.a: Before I would live 'if-then'. If I have money, then I'll be happy. If I drive a sports-car, then I'll be happy. Now I know happiness is rooted in being thankful in every moment.

Sometimes. I was involved in a church, but most church leaderships are more focused on their politics and their own walls around them and money than about Jesus and community and actually helping the local community.

faith.q: What do you say to someone who's lost everything?
faith.a: Ask Jesus to help you. He can change it all.

faith.q: How do you reconcile worship music with a for-profit marketplace?
faith.a: I give a lot for free. I'm not expecting to become a millionaire off of the Selah.fm marketplace. I just want to help artists and creators and run and improve a beautiful platform with a goal that it doesn't cost me any money.

business.q: You've been a millionaire and broke — which taught you more?
business.a: Both taught me a lot about business. Being broke teaches you the fundamentals. You need to make profit. If I have a guitar and I can sing in the streets, I can make a profit.

business.q: What's the worst business advice you ever took?
business.a: That throwing more money at something will solve your problems. Most of time you need to change the roots.

business.q: What did you refuse to compromise on with Selah.fm?

business.a: Selah was just a percentage. For Holy Rave we charge 'Pay What You Want'. It's like a possible donation up front.
Nah not interested in that. We can bootstrap it.

business.q: Unpopular opinion about the creator economy?
business.a: The creators should be rewarded, not the big corporations.
I'm already making music. I will never stop doing that.

artists_promotion.q: What's the biggest lie artists believe about music promotion?
artists_promotion.a: That you need a lot of money to get started. It's about consistency and small steps.

artists_promotion.q: What actually makes a song take off?
artists_promotion.a: Consistency and slowly making the snowball bigger and bigger.

artists_promotion.q: Why do labels take 98% and artists accept it?
artists_promotion.a: Because artists just assume when they sign the contract they've made it and will be rich.

artists_promotion.q: Should artists bother with Spotify playlists?
artists_promotion.a: In the long run, I don't think it's the best option, because the playlist is the 'owner'.

artists_promotion.q: How do fans discover new music?
artists_promotion.a: Short form content. 80% of new music is discovered nowadays through TikTok and Instagram.

artists_promotion.q: One promotion tip for an artist with $100?
artists_promotion.a: If you really only have $100 and that's all you're willing to promote, just spend it on getting your music out there and start sharing it with people.

cpm_data.q: What are actual CPM rates for music promotion?
cpm_data.a: TikTok Creator Fund pays $0.02-0.04 per 1,000 views. YouTube Shorts pays $0.01-0.06 per 1,000 views through the Shorts Fund. Instagram Reels Bonus (invite-only) pays $0.50-1.00 per 1,000 views. On Selah.fm, artists set their own CPM — you can start as low as $0.10 per 1,000 views (that's just $100 for 1M views). Most campaigns range from $0.10 to $10 CPM. Creators can earn around $1,000 per 1M views at the higher end. It's totally up to the artist what they want to offer.

Artists pay 1.20x the creator's CPM. So if a creator earns $1 CPM ($1,000 per 1M views), the artist pays $1.20 CPM. The extra 20% covers platform fees. Artists only pay for verified views — not estimated, not projected. Real views, real payment. Zero upfront cost. And you can start as low as $0.10 CPM if you want to test the waters.

personal.q: What's your daily routine in Tenerife?
personal.a: Coffee, swim, sing, holy rave, promotions, meet up with people, beach, food, little bit on computer.

personal.q: What music are you listening to?
Do you have a partner? Family?
personal.a: Single. 3 kids with 2 mothers, but we're not together. Call with my mother, father and brother every day.
People getting lost and forgetting to give Jesus a try.

personal.q: What do you do for fun?
Where do you want to be in 10 years?
personal.a: No idea. Wherever God wants me to be, that's where I'll be.
